source.version: Published conference paper, CHI '25 (April 26 - May 1, 2025, Yokohama), ACM, DOI 10.1145/3706598.3713886; received 12 September 2024, revised 10 December 2024, accepted 16 January 2025 (p. 17)
source.title_on_document: CreAItive Collaboration? Users' Misjudgment of AI-Creativity Affects Their Collaborative Performance

supplement.where: Referred to as 'Supplementary Materials'; no URL given in the PDF.
supplement.holds: Detailed AUT scoring description (who coded and how), interface screenshots, all questionnaires, informed consent form, detailed descriptive statistics of the sample and bias/confounding analyses, two exemplary human-AI interactions (pp. 5-7, 11). No standard deviations, test statistics, or p-values for the non-significant AUT contrasts appear in the main text; whether the supplement holds them is not stated.

paper_design_summary: 52 dyads (104 second-semester computer science students at Graz University of Technology) were randomly assigned on arrival to do three Alternate Uses Test items together either with access to ChatGPT-4 (26 dyads) or without it (26 dyads). All dyads then did one more AUT item with no AI (immediate post-test), and three weeks later each participant did three AUT items alone online without AI (retention post-test). Outputs were scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration, and groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests.

studies.label: Dyad AUT experiment with and without ChatGPT-4 (main test, immediate post-test, 3-week retention post-test)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to ChatGPT-4 in a chat window inside the AUT interface (copy-paste disabled) versus no AI, during the main test
assignment.quote: Upon arriving at the study location, dyads were randomly assigned to their experimental condition.

arms.name: AI group
arms.description: Dyads performed three AUT items (fork, flower pot, suitcase), 4 minutes each, with off-the-shelf ChatGPT-4 in a chat window; copy-paste from chat into the answer field disabled

arms.name: control non-AI group
arms.description: Dyads performed the same three AUT items without AI

participants.exclusions: The paper calls 52 dyads/104 participants the 'valid sample' and says only native or advanced German-speaking dyads were included in the final sample; it does not state how many dyads were assigned or excluded. Retention post-test counts are not stated separately (Figure 12 is labelled n = 26 dyads per group although the test was individual).
participants.who: Second-semester Computer Science students from an introductory lecture on data science and AI, aged 18-35 (mean 21.55), 77.88 percent male; participants booked slots in pairs, so many dyad partners knew each other (71.43 percent)
participants.quote: The valid sample consisted of 52 dyads/104 participants, with 26 dyads/52 participants per experimental condition.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (off-the-shelf, no prompt engineering by the researchers; reference to OpenAI gpt-4-turbo-and-gpt-4, March 2024)
ai_tool.how_used: Dyads could prompt ChatGPT-4 freely in a chat window during the main test; they had to type answers into the AUT interface because copy-paste was disabled. Dyads accepted 32.91 percent of AI-generated answers (Table 5, p. 12).

task.description: Alternate Uses Test done collaboratively by dyads: main test with three objects (fork, flower pot, suitcase), immediate post-test with one object (glass bottle) without AI, and individual online retention post-test three weeks later with three objects (key, brick, gymnastics ball) without AI
task.duration: 4 minutes per AUT item; on-campus session about one hour; retention post-test three weeks later

company_involvement.description: Authors are affiliated with Graz University of Technology and Know Center Research GmbH (a research center); no AI company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: Dyads were randomly assigned to ChatGPT-4 access versus no AI on the Alternate Uses Test (p. 5); the valid sample is 104 participants in 52 dyads (p. 6), so people exceed 50 although the unit of assignment and of the main analyses is the dyad (52 units, close to the threshold if teams were counted); outcomes are fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration scored on the AUT answers (p. 7).

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT-4, dyads did not differ from no-AI dyads in fluency (14.6 vs 12.7), flexibility (10.0 vs 9.4), or originality (3.7 vs 3.7) but elaborated less (2.1 vs 3.8; U = 924.0, p = 0.005); lower elaboration persisted in the immediate unaided post-test (2.8 vs 4.7; U = 970.0, p = 0.012), and no differences remained three weeks later (pp. 8-10, Figures 4, 8, 12).
open_questions: The Mann-Whitney U values for elaboration (924.0 and 970.0) exceed the maximum possible U for 26 vs 26 dyads (676), so the tests may have been run on participants (52 vs 52) or on item-level scores rather than dyads; the analysis unit and hence the n behind the tests is unclear.
Retention post-test sample size is not stated; it was individual, yet Figure 12 is labelled n = 26 dyads per group, and attrition over three weeks is not reported.
Number of dyads assigned before the German-language restriction (n randomized) is not stated.
Whether the preregistration names a primary outcome: hypotheses H1-H3 cover flexibility and originality only, which I marked preregistered_primary; fluency and elaboration were not hypothesized.
notes: Outcomes marked preregistered_primary are those named in the preregistered hypotheses H1-H3 (flexibility and originality; p. 4); the paper does not use the word 'primary'. Main-test means are mean indices over three AUT items; immediate post-test is one item. Other outcomes not listed because they are not creativity contrasts: prompt specificity coding (Tables 1, 3, 4), AI-answer acceptance rate (Table 5) and its within-AI-group correlation with fluency (rho_s = 0.424, p = 0.002; p. 11, Figure 14), and self-reported perception of AI (Figure 13). Section heading 4.5 text is duplicated in the PDF as 4.5.1 and 4.5.2 (p. 7). A pre-study comparing 10 AI chatbots with 20 human dyads on the AUT (Section 4.1, p. 4) is published separately [7] and has no assignment of AI to people; it is not coded here.
